title: Metallic sample preparation for phase transformation analysis
author: Paganotti, Bessa, et al.

steps.title: Cut ingot slice
steps.instruction: Use a precision disc cutter to cut a slice perpendicular to the major axis of the ingot; the slice size should be large enough that mass loss is negligible but small enough to avoid excessive material use.

steps.title: Choose surface handling
steps.instruction: Decide whether to embed the cut slice in resin (to increase handling ease and base area) or to work with the bare slice; both options require subsequent surface preparation.

steps.title: Initial sanding sequence
steps.instruction: Place a SiC sanding‑paper disk on a spinning metal disk that is continuously water‑cooled; lightly press the sample onto the paper and sand using progressively finer grits, starting at 200 grit and moving to 400, 600, 800 and finally 1000 grit (or up to 1200 grit if higher finish is required).

substeps.instruction: Orient the sample so that the scratches produced are orthogonal to the tangential speed of the disk (Fig. 9a).
When all scratches become parallel to the tangential speed, change to the next finer grit and re‑orient the sample orthogonal to the speed (Fig. 9b).
Repeat until the desired surface finish is achieved.

steps.title: Evaluate finish orientation
steps.instruction: After each grit change, verify that the new scratches are parallel to the tangential speed before proceeding; this ensures complete removal of the previous grit’s scratches.

steps.title: Polish after sanding
steps.instruction: Place a polishing cloth on the same spinning metal disk; apply a small amount of polishing compound to the cloth and press the sample against it.

substeps.instruction: If using diamond‑based compound, add a lubricant consisting of a 1:2 vol ratio glycerin : ethanol; if using alumina‑based compound, use water as lubricant.
Polish sequentially with diamond compounds of particle sizes 15 µm, 9 µm, 6 µm, 3 µm, 1 µm and finally 0.25 µm.
If finer finish is required, after the 0.25 µm diamond step polish with alumina compounds of 1 µm, 0.3 µm and 0.05 µm.
During polishing, monitor the surface with an optical microscope; change to a finer compound only when all visible scratches are parallel to the radial speed of the disk.

steps.title: Select polishing compound type
steps.instruction: Choose among chromium‑oxide, synthetic‑diamond, or alumina polishing compounds; note that chromium‑oxide is cheapest but toxic, diamond is easiest to handle and does not impregnate plastics, while alumina can impregnate metal surfaces and affect EDS measurements.

steps.title: Punch smaller disks (optional)
steps.instruction: If a smaller specimen is required, place the polished slice into a die‑punch set and press to obtain a disk of the desired diameter (e.g., 4 mm for DSC T‑zero pan, 3 mm for Setaram alumina crucible). After punching, polish one side of the disk using the sanding‑and‑polishing sequence described above.

steps.title: Prepare etching solutions
steps.instruction: Prepare the required etching solution according to Table 1, using distilled or ultrapure water; follow the specific preparation notes for each solution.

substeps.instruction: Iron‑chloride solution: dissolve 17 g FeCl₃·6H₂O(s) in 93 mL H₂O(l) then add 25 mL concentrated HCl (≈37 %).
Nital: mix 10 mL HNO₃(aq) (≈68 %) with cold ethanol; keep refrigerated, keep total concentration <10 % (if higher, replace ethanol with methanol, limiting exposure to 0.002 g methanol · m⁻³ air).
Chloral: mix 90 mL C₂H₅OH(l) with 2 mL HCl (≈37 %).
Aqua regia: mix 98 mL C₂H₅OH(l) with 10 mL HCl (≈37 %).
Ammonium persulfate I: prepare 50 mL saturated (NH₄)₂S₂O₈(s) solution at room temperature, add water to 75 mL total, then add 50 mL H₂O₂(l) as the final step.
Ammonium persulfate II: dissolve 10 g (NH₄)₂S₂O₈(s) in 100 mL H₂O(l).
All solutions: store in a freezer at ≤ ‑18 °C, never in hermetic containers, and keep in a fume hood with PPE.

steps.title: Etch the sample
steps.instruction: Degrease the polished sample with acetone, then drop the chosen etching solution onto the surface using a pipette; control the reaction time precisely (as short as 1 s) and monitor contrast under an optical microscope.

substeps.instruction: If adequate contrast is not achieved, repeat a short etch (e.g., another 1 s) and re‑examine.
When the desired contrast is obtained, wash the sample with water or ethanol, dry with a compressed‑air pistol, and proceed to analysis.
If over‑etched, sand the surface again, re‑polish, and re‑etch; if only slightly over‑etched, re‑polish without further sanding.

steps.title: Use stored etchants
steps.instruction: Remove an aliquot of the refrigerated solution into a non‑sealed flask, let it equilibrate to ambient temperature in a fume hood, then test on a calibration sample before using on unknown specimens.

substeps.instruction: Maintain ambient temperature and humidity between 50 % and 90 % during etching for reproducibility.
Remember that warmer solutions etch faster; adjust exposure time accordingly.

steps.title: Prepare sample for specific analysis
steps.instruction: Tailor the final preparation to the intended characterization technique:

substeps.instruction: Optical microscopy: sand, polish, and etch as described.
Thermal analysis (DSC, DTA): polishing and etching are not required; use the appropriate disk size (4 mm for DSC, 3 mm for DTA).
Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM): ensure all polishing compounds are thoroughly removed; avoid alumina residues that can interfere with EDS or back‑scattered imaging.
Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM): thin the sample to micron or nanometer thickness using specialized thinning techniques performed by a trained technician.
